newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's small brokers may face loss amid buffeting.
newsitem.headline: Japan's small brokers may face loss amid buffeting.

text.p: Japan's second-tier brokers are being buffeted by less-than-expected trade volume as they cling to dwindling market share, and some may forecast losses on Thursday for the first half of the business year, analysts say.

"Management of second-tier brokers must want profits to match losses. But it would probably be difficult for some to do so for the first half due to poorer-than-expected stock business in July, August and early September," said an analyst at a second-tier brokerage, who declined to be named.
"It's becoming hard for many second-tier brokers to take high risks trading stocks and bonds after the protracted stock market slump that lasted until recently," he also said.
All 10 of the second-tier brokers made bullish earnings projections in May, expecting parent profits for the first half, from April 1 to September 30.

But many of the 10 firms, whose customers are small investors still reluctant to put their money into stocks despite relatively stable stock prices, will revise their forecasts downward and some may be in the red, analysts said.
The 10 are Sanyo, New Japan, Kankaku, Wako, Okasan, Yamatane, Cosmo, Dai-Ichi, Tokyo and Kokusai Securities.
On Tuesday, Nikko Securities, one of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages, took the lead in revising its forecast downward.

Nikko's managing director Katsuyuki Ishiohmaru told reporters that lower-than-expected volume in stock and convertible bond (CB) trading on the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) was a major reason to cut its projections.

Average daily turnover on the Tokyo exchange was 430.5 billion yen ($3.91 billion) in the first five months of 1996/97, against Nikko's previous assumption that first-half turnover would be 500 billion yen ($4.54 billion), he said.

Tokyo stock prices have recovered since late last year, when foreign and institutional investors stepped up stock buying as Japanese economic prospects brightened and the nation's problem loan woes eased. But stock prices slipped and turnover began falling sharply in July amid fears of interest rate rises and darker economic prospects, brokers said.

Nikko now expects parent current profit for the six months to September 30 of 20 billion yen ($181 million), down from its May forecast of 38 billion yen ($345 million) and an actual 25.50 billion yen ($231 million) in the same period last year.
Parent current profit is pre-tax, and includes losses and gains on non-operating activities.
Analysts said another big broker, Yamaichi, would also lower its earnings forecast as it had expected average daily turnover of about 480 billion yen ($4.36 billion) in 1996/97.
Two other big brokerages -- Nomura and Daiwa -- did not announce any forecasts in May as they adopt a policy of not making earnings forecasts.
The impact of stock volume is much bigger for second-tier brokerages than the Big Four.
The Big Four depend on commissions on stock transactions for about 30 percent of their revenue. But commissions account for 60 to 70 percent of revenues for the second-tier brokerages, analysts said.

"The industry is facing deregulation of stockbroking fees. To cope with liberalisation, second-tier brokers had better withdraw from unprofitable business to lower break-even points for profits and losses," said an analyst at a big brokerage.
"They (second-tier brokers) have not benefited from an expansion in the primary market seen this year as borrowers go to big brokerages and securities arms of banks," he added. ($1=110 yen)
